scenes.heading: Persistence
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Persistence and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What persist adds over cache
items: Control memory vs disk vs serialization
scenes.narration: Persistence is the general form of caching that lets you pick exactly how and where Spark keeps your data. While cache always uses memory-and-disk, persist accepts a StorageLevel so you can trade memory for disk, choose serialization, or even replicate blocks. That control matters when data is too big to fit comfortably in memory.

scenes.heading: Common storage levels
scenes.narration: MEMORY_ONLY keeps deserialized objects for the fastest reads but simply recomputes partitions that do not fit. MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER stores serialized bytes, which are more compact and can spill to disk when memory runs short. The serialized levels reduce memory pressure and garbage collection at the cost of some CPU to deserialize on read.

scenes.code:
from pyspark import StorageLevel

features = build_features(spark)  # expensive pipeline
features.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER)
features.count()  # materialize

model_a = train(features)
model_b = train_alt(features)
features.unpersist()
scenes.heading: Choosing a level explicitly
scenes.narration: Here an expensive feature pipeline is persisted with a serialized memory-and-disk level, which keeps a big dataset in a compact form and spills gracefully if memory is tight. The count materializes it, and both training runs then reuse the stored data. Choosing the serialized level here avoids GC thrash that MEMORY_ONLY might cause on large data. As always, unpersist releases the resources when done.

scenes.text: Match the StorageLevel to your data size and read pattern.
scenes.narration: For big reused datasets prefer serialized memory-and-disk; reserve memory-only for small, hot data. Always unpersist to return memory to the executors.
